early-shadows.title: Watch a hand’s shadow
early-shadows.invitation: Make a hand shadow and see what catches their eye.
early-shadows.summary: Hold your hand with light behind it and let its shadow offer something for your baby to notice.
early-shadows.cue: Your baby is awake, comfortable and interested in looking.
detail: The authors include hand shadows among the simple things a young baby can watch. Notice where their gaze settles and give them time to look.

They also describe light and shadow moving through leaves and branches, or a high-contrast picture within the baby’s view. Follow the interest you see; looking away or becoming upset is a reason to stop or change what is offered.

baby-movement.title: Room for their own movement
baby-movement.invitation: The authors make room for the baby’s own awake movement, with comfort and help close by.
baby-movement.summary: The authors favor awake movement that the baby initiates, with room to explore, help when needed, and no propping into sitting or standing before they can get there themselves.
baby-movement.cue: Notice how your baby moves now, what catches their attention, and when effort becomes frustration.
detail: Davies and Uzodike describe a prepared space where a baby can explore their own movements. A nearby object may invite a reach or a change of direction; the point is to follow the baby’s present interest and pace.

Their caution is about propping a baby into sitting or standing. They separately describe awake time on both the back and tummy, while noticing discomfort and changing things or picking the baby up when needed.

When effort turns to frustration, they describe coming closer and offering enough help for the baby to continue. Their activity ages are guides, and they explicitly welcome seeking support for developmental concerns.

baby-language.title: A conversation with your baby
baby-language.invitation: Answer their sound, then leave a little room for the reply.
baby-language.summary: Answer a sound, smile or gesture, then pause. Your baby’s next response can guide the conversation.
baby-language.cue: Your baby is watching your face or experimenting with sounds.
detail: Come where your baby can see your face. Say something, listen, and leave a little space for their sound or movement. You can echo a sound, smile back, or put a few words to what seems to interest them.
Raspberries, bubbles and changes in volume are part of the vocal play the authors describe. There is no need to ask for a particular sound or word.

For families who choose baby signs, the book suggests pairing a few familiar spoken words with signs, such as “milk” or “done.” Its age labels differ between sections; the authors’ wider guidance is to notice the baby’s response and interest.
